data.title: South Korea becomes fourth country globally to hit US$1 trillion exports on AI chip boom
data.description: SEOUL: South Korea's exports so far for this year have exceeded US$1 trillion, driven by a global AI chip boom, making it the fourth country in the world to reach the milestone after Germany, the United States and China. Exports passed the US$1 trillion mark on Thursday (Nov 19), compared with last year's record of US$709 billion, the trade ministry said. Asia's fourth-largest economy, home to leading chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, is riding the global boom in AI investment that is fuelling exports and investments. Still, domestic demand remains weak with the benefits of the export boom yet to trickle down to many households. Consumer sentiment has been hurt by high interest rates and prices, as well as unprecedented volatility in the domestic stock market. "Now, we need to turn this achievement into sustainable growth. We will enhance the competitiveness of major industries and grow future growth engines, such as AI and bio," President Lee Jae Myung said in a social media post on X. "Most of all, the achievement in exports should improve the lives of the people. We will create 'growth for all', sharing the opportunities and fruits of growth with big and small companies as well as the capital area and regional areas," Lee said. The Lee administration plans to create a 162.3 trillion won (US$121.94 billion) Future Response Fund to funnel excess tax revenue from the chip boom toward growth industries, young people, regional development and education. South Korea's economic growth is expected to quicken to the mid-3 per cent range this year on record chip exports , after expanding 1 per cent last year, the country's finance minister said last month.

data.title: GTA VI to supercharge Sony - just not in Japan
data.description: TOKYO: The global launch of Grand Theft Auto VI on Thursday (Nov 19) is expected to provide a major boost to PlayStation maker Sony - albeit not in its home market of Japan, where the franchise is a niche pursuit. The long-awaited open-world crime action game from Take-Two Interactive's Rockstar Games is rolling out across the world and has been met with rave reviews and fans taking time off work to play. Three-quarters of the 17 million GTA VI units sold are on PlayStation, according to estimates from Sensor Tower, outselling Xbox maker Microsoft. Shares in Sony, whose PlayStation 5 console is in its seventh year on the market, were up 2.8 per cent in Tokyo compared with flat trading in the benchmark index.Analysts think that momentum is unlikely to extend to Japan, where Switch 2 maker Nintendo dominates the gaming device market and consumers prefer anime-style titles to realistic, violent Western games. "The current trends in Japan don't really fit this kind of game," said Toyo Securities analyst Hideki Yasuda. "It won't sell much in Japan, but there's absolutely no need for this game to sell in Japan," he said. Earlier this year Sony scored a major global success with movie Spider-Man: Brand New Day but in Japan faced competition from breakout hit Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of Mermaid Island. Analysts expect the release of GTA VI to soften the decline of PS5 hardware sales this year and support growth in software sales. Sony sold 2.6 million PS5 units during the July to September quarter, which analysts see as reflecting demand ahead of GTA VI, down from 4 million a year earlier. "We've modeled PlayStation profits materially ahead of the Street in the next couple of quarters, on account of the 'GTA VI' launch," Bernstein analyst David Dai wrote in a note. The release is bolstering Sony's games slate after it delayed the launch of God of War Laufey by three months to May 2027. Sony is grappling with procurement challenges as the cost of memory chips has risen sharply due to the AI boom. "I don't get the sense that Sony has much desire to aggressively sell hardware ... the benefits Sony gets from royalties will be enormous," said Toyo Securities' Yasuda.

data.title: Challenger says revised Daiichi Life takeover offer falls short, shares down
data.description: Nov 19 : Challenger rebuffed an improved takeover proposal from a unit of Japan's Daiichi Life that valued the Australian investment manager at A$8.17 billion ($5.48 billion), sending its shares to a four-week low on Thursday. Daiichi Life's revised offer for the remaining 79.5 per cent of Challenger shares it does not already own was A$12.20 apiece, a 2.1 per cent premium to the stock's last close and 40 Australian cents above its previous offer. Challenger's board said the revised offer from the Japanese insurer does not "adequately represent fair value" for shareholders in the context of a control transaction. Daiichi Life did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Challenger's shares slid as much as 2.7 per cent to A$11.63 in early Sydney trade, their lowest level since October 22. They were last down 2.1 per cent as of 0228 GMT, compared with a 0.8 per cent decline in the broader market. "The Challenger board, in our view, would be open to a deal, but the premium would clearly need to be higher to start the deal process formally," said Cameron Curko, CIO at Pitcher Partners Sydney. The strength of their underlying business of late gives them a "strong hand" to demand more, he added. TAL Daiichi Life Australia Pty currently owns 20.47 per cent of Challenger, LSEG data showed. Japan's appetite for Australian dealmaking is hardly new. ORIX Corp and a Sumitomo Corp-led consortium were among those vying for vehicle leasing company FleetPartners. Local media reported last month that Suncorp and suitor Tokio Marine had engaged in preliminary takeover discussions, a report the Australian insurer subsequently denied. ($1 = 1.4896 Australian dollars)

data.title: BOJ chief plays down soft consumption data, signals near-term rate hike
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 19 : Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda on Thursday reiterated the central bank's resolve to keep raising interest rates, saying financial conditions remain loose despite past hikes. "It's important to anchor underlying inflation around our 2 per cent target to avoid risk of an inflation overshoot from materialising and hurting the economy," Ueda told parliament.

data.title: Arizona says it is investigating OpenAI, other firms over possible rogue agents
data.description: CHICAGO, Nov 18 : The state of Arizona has opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI and other AI companies relating to the "apparent infiltration of banks by rogue AI agents," Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes said Wednesday. A criminal investigation does not necessarily mean charges will be brought. Mayes said her office was investigating whether Arizona state law was being violated on an ongoing basis.  "The state of Arizona is very worried about this, and we are looking at it from multiple angles," Mayes told a press conference in Chicago. Mayes declined to identify the other companies her office was investigating. She said her office had been in contact with Arizona banks, but declined to name them or give their responses. A spokesperson for OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The banking industry has become increasingly concerned that sophisticated AI agents could harm the banking system and the institutions trusted to hold people's wealth. Reuters reported last month that major US banks have been blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside customer accounts and making transactions.  Mayes' comments come two days after California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI for allegedly developing a dangerous product ‌without adequate safety procedures or oversight after reports that its AI models had carried out cyberattacks independently. OpenAI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on that lawsuit, but the company has ⁠acknowledged a general need for more transparency around rogue AI behavior and said it was reinforcing its safeguards. On September 16, the company published a new framework for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the side of transparency “even when significance is uncertain.”

data.title: UK finance sector cyber incidents hit second-highest level in five years
data.description: LONDON, Nov 19 : Cyber incidents reported to Britain's financial watchdog in October hit their second-highest monthly level in five years, underscoring the growing threat facing the financial sector. The Financial Conduct Authority said the number of incidents reported in October was more than 50 per cent higher than the previous peak recorded 18 months earlier. The FCA, together with the Bank of England, also proposed new guidance aimed at giving banks, insurers and other financial firms clearer expectations on how to prepare for, detect and recover from cyberattacks. Earlier this month, French lender Credit Mutuel Arkéa said hackers had stolen around €100 million ($113 million) in a cyber heist, while crypto exchange Binance said hackers had drained $6.3 billion of digital assets. Katharine Braddick, chief executive of Britain's Prudential Regulation Authority and deputy governor at the Bank of England, said cyberattacks were becoming more frequent, complex and damaging. "Regulators need confidence both that firms have strong cyber controls and that they can detect, contain and recover quickly from incidents," she said. The total of 38 incidents reported to the FCA in October was the second highest in five years, surpassed only by the 49 reported in June 2023 during the MOVEit data breach. The proposed guidance sets out more detailed expectations on cyber resilience, governance, incident response, recovery and supply-chain risks. It builds on existing operational resilience requirements rather than introducing new regulatory obligations. A consultation closes on February 26. The regulators also issued additional guidance on managing cyber risks linked to frontier AI and future advances in quantum computing.

data.title: US Department of Justice charges Russian for targeting Palantir as foreign agent
data.description: WASHINGTON, Nov 18 : A federal grand jury has indicted a Russian national on charges of acting as a foreign agent to target the technology and defense company Palantir and surveil its employees, according to court documents and two people familiar with the matter. Working with Russian collaborators, Igor D'iu allegedly traveled from Russia and stalked employees of what the Justice Department described in its affidavit and press release only as a Silicon Valley technology and defense company. Two people familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, identified the company as Palantir Technologies Inc, which has a large office in Palo Alto, California but is based in Florida.  D'iu took photos of employees' computer screens while at a coffee shop near company offices, according to the affidavit. He also followed a female staff member nearly 30 miles (50 km)  but stopped his pursuit after the employee contacted the police, prosecutors said. “The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company’s assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia,” Craig H. Missakian, the top federal prosecutor in San Francisco, said in a statement. Palantir CEO Alex Karp has publicly backed Ukraine, and the company has said it deployed its technology to the country. Palantir did not respond to a request for comment. Russia's embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment. One of the people, who is familiar with the company's thinking, said the attempted breach was unsuccessful and will not change the company's support for Ukraine. The person added that Palantir is unlikely to be the only technology and defense company targeted by the Russians. News of the alleged surveillance comes amid heightened scrutiny of tech company security after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned in the wake of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of having Chinese intelligence ties. D'iu, who is being held in federal custody, is charged with two counts related to his alleged work as a Russian agent, one count of interstate stalking and one count of fraud related to identification documents. He faces up to 21 years in prison. Reuters could not immediately determine if he had appointed a lawyer.  Bloomberg first reported that Palantir was the target of the Russian surveillance campaign.  D'iu allegedly entered the United States through the Texas-Mexico border in July and searched for company employee addresses online in August, according to the indictment. After following two employees on consecutive days out of the company's Palo Alto offices in early September, he was contacted by local law enforcement. FBI agents later found a falsified US passport, Russian passports, roughly $18,000 in cash and 10 handwritten addresses, at least five of which were linked with employees' home addresses. Prosecutors said his co-conspirators told him he was working for "the Motherland" and directed him to set up his computer near the tech company's offices so they could try to obtain information from nearby employees.  He is next scheduled to appear in court on Tuesday.

data.title: US lawmakers seek Microsoft briefing on reported AI deal talks with ByteDance
data.description: A United States House panel asked Microsoft on Wednesday (Nov 18) to brief lawmakers on a report which said the company could allow the Chinese firm ByteDance to use OpenAI models through Microsoft's Azure cloud platform. Technology news outlet the Information reported that Microsoft was nearing a US$500 million deal with ByteDance. The chairman of the House Select Committee on China, John Moolenaar, said the panel wanted more details "given serious concerns over American companies helping China catch up to the US in the AI race". "Microsoft takes misuse of its AI services seriously and is committed to enforcing its terms of service, complying with applicable laws, and honouring its partner agreements," a Microsoft spokesperson said, adding that the company does not comment on confidential customer negotiations. Washington has stressed the need for the US to be ahead of China in the AI race. In recent weeks, media reports about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy have increased scrutiny on technology business ties. Moolenaar, a Michigan Republican, said it was unacceptable for Microsoft, as a Pentagon contractor, to sell AI services to ByteDance.  "Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance," Moolenaar said in a statement.  "Leading American technology companies should not be playing both sides of the US-China AI race." Microsoft is also pursuing deals to sell OpenAI models to other Chinese businesses, including Alibaba, according to the Information report.  OpenAI prevents most Chinese firms from using its AI, but Microsoft has the rights to sell OpenAI's technology and does not impose the same restrictions, the Information said.

data.title: Hot demand lifts Anthropic IPO price to US$83 a share: Reports
data.description: NEW YORK: Anthropic priced its initial public offering at US$83 a share on Wednesday (Nov 18), above its expected range, US media reported, as hot demand for the artificial intelligence giant brushed aside market jitters over the spy scandal that toppled Nvidia's chief executive. At that price, the sale of 825 million shares would raise about US$68.5 billion and value the maker of the Claude chatbot at about US$1.5 trillion, including employee stock options and restricted shares. The listing gives ordinary investors their first chance to bet directly on a stand-alone AI giant. Trading is expected to begin Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT". Anthropic had set a range of US$70 to US$78 a share last week. Institutional investors placed about US$400 billion in orders for the shares and retail investors about US$100 billion, according to CNBC, leaving the offering roughly eight times oversubscribed at the top of the initial range.The strong demand comes even as AI stocks have swung sharply, with investors questioning whether heavy spending on the technology will pay off. Nvidia, the chip giant at the centre of the AI investment boom and an investor in Anthropic and dozens of other AI companies, has been shaken by the resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang after he admitted to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence reportedly believes could be a Chinese spy . “Anthropic’s IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning,” Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co said in a note, adding that Nvidia’s troubles had cast a shadow over the sector at a time when investors were very nervous about tech stocks. Wall Street is also digesting the US midterm election results, which gave control of both chambers of Congress to Democrats, who are more wary of AI. Earlier estimates had put Anthropic's valuation as high as US$2 trillion, but they fell as AI stocks slid on Wall Street in recent weeks. Anthropic's Claude models are among the most powerful in the world, hailed for their potential to help cure diseases and solve hard problems but also feared for their capacity to destabilise societies and replace human workers. The five-year-old company's revenue has surged at a pace few US companies have ever matched, reaching US$17 billion in the third quarter, up from US$1.4 billion a year earlier. Much of that revenue comes from customers paying to use its AI models for computer coding. Siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, now the company’s chief executive and president, founded Anthropic with several colleagues in 2021 after leaving ChatGPT-maker OpenAI. The offering falls short of the record US$75 billion that Elon Musk’s SpaceX raised in June at a valuation of US$1.77 trillion. SpaceX’s total later rose to US$86 billion after its underwriters exercised an option to buy additional shares. Seven tech companies, including Google, Nvidia, AMD and Microsoft, have agreed to buy US$26 billion of non-voting shares at the IPO price in a separate private placement. The companies are investors in Anthropic or major suppliers of its computing power and have a lot riding on the IPO."CATASTROPHIC RISK" Anthropic's IPO filing gives extensive detail to the risks of the technology, reflecting the company’s focus on safety even as it builds ever more powerful models. US Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren criticised the listing on X, saying the company "fails to answer for the potential threats to Americans’ retirements and the entire financial system if this IPO goes awry". The filing also warns that advanced AI systems "could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly". It also says the company's public positions on AI regulation and safety could expose it to political backlash. The warning refers to Anthropic’s feud with the Trump administration, which ordered federal agencies to stop using its technology and labelled it a supply-chain risk after the company refused to let the Pentagon use Claude for domestic mass surveillance or lethal autonomous weapons.

data.title: Anthropic IPO to mint thousands of millionaires
data.description: NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Anthropic's initial public offering is poised to create thousands of paper millionaires among current and former employees, in what could rank among the largest employee wealth windfalls in Silicon Valley history.   The offering is expected to unleash a wave of new wealth across the AI sector, rewarding everyone from early researchers and engineers to administrative staff who received stock grants as the Claude maker raced from startup to one of the world's most valuable companies. The IPO filing shows the amount of wealth embedded in employee stock awards, but not how that wealth is distributed among workers. As a result, outside estimates vary widely. Hill, a San Francisco marketplace for private-company shares, estimates 598 non-founder employees will hold at least $100 million in equity after the initial public offering, which is slated to open on the Nasdaq on Thursday at $83 a share, above its initial target range that would value the company at up to $1.4 trillion, according to a person familiar with the information. Private-markets research firm Sacra estimates that roughly 2,800 current and former Anthropic employees could hold at least $1 million of pretax vested equity at a $1.35 trillion valuation, the middle of the price range.  The firms say their estimates are model-based and use public information. Reuters could not independently verify the estimates, which reflect factors including vesting periods, exercises, tender transactions, option awards, restricted stock units, award timing, headcount and employee retention rates. The filing does not disclose sums due individuals. But the wealth potentially shared by employees is vast.  Anthropic option holders were sitting on $119 billion of paper gains as of September 30, at a weighted average exercise price of $2.91 per share, the company disclosed. About $73 billion of that amount had vested through service and could be exercised immediately.  Anthropic did not respond to a comment request on the estimates. "The idea of equity appreciating to an amount that is life-changing is something that people strive for," Hill CEO Andrew Benson said. "It doesn't get better than this." EQUITY AT ENTRY LEVEL Workers who joined the firm when it started five years ago —  even in administrative positions and entry-level jobs — could be sitting on life-changing wealth, reflecting their holdings of stock options that carry exercise prices of less than $1.  Options granted through 2023 and still outstanding at the end of that year carried an average exercise price of 52 cents, the filing shows.  At SpaceX, which was founded in 2002 and went  public in June in a record-busting IPO, many of the employees who became millionaires had worked there for more than a decade.    "Early employees who started in a very junior role should have actually a better financial outcome than somebody who joined in a very senior role right before the IPO," Benson said, referring to Anthropic. Non-founder Anthropic employees can sell up to 10 per cent of their holdings on the first trading day, and up to another 35 per cent after fiscal 2026 earnings. EARLY HIRES REAP REWARDS Founded in 2021, the Claude maker expanded its workforce rapidly alongside the AI boom, growing to about 5,300 employees as of September 30 from roughly 940 at the end of 2024. As it hired aggressively, the company used stock-based compensation as a key recruiting tool. A May 2024 job posting for an administrative business partner role shows how the benefits of Anthropic's stock awards extended beyond AI researchers and engineers.  The position, which involved scheduling and managing calendars for company leaders, coordinating conference logistics and handling expense claims and reimbursements, paid an annual salary of $140,000 to $190,000.  The posting added that equity would be "a major component of the total compensation" beyond the salary, indicating that administrative and support staff were also eligible for stock awards alongside cash pay. That year, Anthropic said it granted employees options at an average exercise price of $1.30 per share. "And as we know from several anecdotes after the SpaceX IPO, this is often enough to help people down the organization chart do quite well in IPO," said Marcelo Ballve, head of research at Sacra. Anthropic granted CFO Krishna Rao 14 million stock options in 2024, also with a $1.30 exercise price, according to the filing. At the IPO price range, those options would carry roughly $1 billion in gross intrinsic value, before exercise costs and taxes. Ballve said that equity awards for administrative, support and entry-level roles are not uncommon at venture capital-backed companies. Historically, though, many companies phased out equity grants at hiring for these roles as they scaled up and salaries became more competitive, moving to performance- and tenure-based grants instead. After Anthropic goes public, the company will likely reserve upfront equity grants solely for recruiting top talent, he said.

data.title: Palo Alto raises annual forecast, signs $4.5 billion deal for Applied Compute
data.description: Nov 18 : Cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks raised its annual revenue forecast and signed a deal to acquire AI startup Applied Compute in a deal valued at $4.5 billion, as a heightened threat environment pushes customers toward broader security products. Shares of Palo Alto jumped about 10 per cent in after-hours trading to $368.60, and drove gains in rivals. CrowdStrike rose 5.3 per cent, Zscaler climbed 3 per cent and Fortinet gained 2.1 per cent. Palo Alto Networks has been repositioning itself as an integrated cybersecurity provider, with recent deals, including its $3.35 billion acquisition of cloud management and monitoring firm Chronosphere and an agreement with Israeli startup Koi. The company is looking to tap growing cybersecurity spending as the rapid adoption of AI creates new security risks, giving attackers new ways to exploit vulnerabilities. "As AI accelerates cyber attacks, enterprises are moving with urgency to replace disjointed tools with unified platforms," Palo Alto CEO Nikesh Arora said during the company's analyst call on Wednesday. With the acquisition of Applied Compute, Palo Alto is looking to offer users a technology platform to help customers securely train and deploy open-weight models as they expand their use of AI. Open-weight models, AI systems whose trained settings are publicly released, present security challenges, including the risk of model tampering, data leakage and misuse by bad actors. "Applied Compute extends Palo Alto's push beyond traditional cybersecurity into enterprise AI. The opportunity is to bring AI infrastructure and security closer together," said Shaul Eyal, analyst at TD Cowen. The deal is expected to close in the third quarter of fiscal 2027. Palo Alto now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to be between $14.52 billion and $14.57 billion, compared with its prior expectation of $14.10 billion to $14.20 billion. Its first-quarter revenue came in at $3.45 billion, up 39 per cent from a year earlier, beating estimates of $3.31 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.

data.title: Stocks slip with eyes on Anthropic and Nvidia, oil prices slide
data.description: NEW YORK/LONDON, Nov 18 : A gauge of stocks across the globe fell on Wednesday after Nvidia's quarterly results and ahead of Anthropic's market debut, while the dollar's strength on the back of a hawkish Federal Reserve weighed on trader sentiment. The dollar index strengthened to a fresh 19-month high after US Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller told CNBC the central bank needs to either approve a half-point interest rate hike at its December meeting or communicate a faster pace of hikes in 2027. Mining stocks dragged European shares lower, while Nvidia's results initially helped Asian shares, with South Korea's Kospi up 2 per cent overnight. But the Nvidia rally fizzled and its stock fell 2.9 per cent after rising as much as 2.7 per cent. Nvidia's board dismissed the idea of rehiring former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week. The company's results and strong outlook did not dispel uncertainty. "We believe (Tuesday's) results have stabilized sentiment and put a floor under the recent AI selloff, but they have postponed rather than permanently cured investor anxiety," said Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.11 per cent to 50,198.17, the S&P 500 lost 0.23 per cent to 7,323.63 and the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.42 per cent to 24,429.89.  MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe fell 0.45 per cent to 1,074.61. The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 1.03 per cent, while emerging market stocks fell 0.2 per cent. Japan's Nikkei rose 0.28 per cent to 59,024.28. The next health check on the AI industry will come as Anthropic prepares its market debut on Thursday. The company priced its initial public offering on Wednesday at $83 per share, above the expected range, according to a person familiar with the matter. DOLLAR UP, OIL DOWN In currencies, the dollar strengthened as Waller's comments and recent economic data cemented expectations for an interest rate hike next month. "The Federal Reserve seems at the moment to be very determined to hike interest rates and maybe even aggressively do so," said Juan Perez, senior director of trading at Monex USA in Washington. "That's the belief right now that's carrying the US dollar." The dollar index rose 0.17 per cent to 103.79, with the euro down 0.22 per cent at $1.0973. In commodities markets, crude prices fell after US crude and fuel inventories rose more than expected, adding to expectations of a supply surplus.  US crude lost 3.3 per cent to $83.17 a barrel and Brent fell to $91.84 per barrel, down 1.4 per cent. Spot gold dropped 3.24 per cent to $3,725.10 an ounce and spot silver fell 4.98 per cent to $45.04 an ounce. Copper declined 4.54 per cent to $12,626.00 a ton. Yields on 2-year US Treasury notes, which are sensitive to interest rate expectations, edged higher on hawkish Fed speaker comments and minutes from the last monetary policy committee meeting that underscored inflation worries. The 2-year note yield rose 1.31 basis points to 4.802 per cent, from 4.789 per cent late on Tuesday, while the benchmark US 10-year note yield fell 3.47 basis points to 5.068 per cent, from 5.103 per cent.

data.title: Anthropic prices blockbuster IPO at $83 a share, source says
data.description: Nov 18 : Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, above its targeted range of $70 to $78 per share on Wednesday, in one of the largest stock-market IPOs on record and the first by a major frontier artificial intelligence model developer, according to a person familiar with the matter. The size of the offering has increased, the person said, asking not to be identified because the information isn’t public. The pricing makes Anthropic's sale the second mega-IPO of the year with a focus on AI, following June's SpaceX sale, as investors jump at the chance for exposure to the fast-growing industry, even as the industry also faces mounting questions over the cost of developing and operating artificial intelligence models. The AI lab comes to the public market just months after SpaceX's record-setting IPO, but the backdrop for AI stocks has turned more challenging. Chipmakers and cloud companies central to the business have come under pressure in recent weeks due to valuation concerns, mounting AI infrastructure costs, and the sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, a key pillar of the industry's growth.  The pricing follows a roadshow that attracted demand exceeding several multiples of the number of shares offered, Reuters previously reported, despite questions about the company's outlook and its ability to sustain rapid growth as competition in the AI industry intensifies. Anthropic's closest rival, OpenAI, is also expected to pursue a public listing as early as next year. Anthropic declined to comment.  Bloomberg news first reported on the pricing.

data.title: Palo Alto to buy AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5 billion
data.description: Nov 18 : Cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks said on Wednesday it will acquire AI startup Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion, as it seeks to help businesses securely deploy open-weight artificial intelligence models. Shares of Palo Alto rose 8.5 per cent in after hours trading. The latest deal adds to a run of 2026 acquisitions by Palo Alto, including identity-security company CyberArk and observability firm Chronosphere, as the company pushes into AI. Applied Compute sells software that helps companies adapt and run open-weight models, AI systems whose trained settings are publicly released, on their own data. The deal is expected to close in the third quarter of fiscal 2027. Separately, Palo Alto said it expects fiscal 2027 revenue to be between $14.52 billion and $14.57 billion, above analysts' average estimate of $14.16 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.
